He comes down on the lawn to hide his face from her. She follows him caressingly.
Poor Ricky Ticky Tavy! Poor heart!
It belongs to you, Ann. Forgive me: I must speak of it. I love you. You know I love you.
What’s the good, Tavy? You know that my mother is determined that I shall marry Jack.
But you are not bound to sacrifice yourself always to the wishes of your parents.
My father loved me. My mother loves me. Surely their wishes are a better guide than my own selfishness.

Oh, I know how unselfish you are, Ann. But believe me﻿—though I know I am speaking in my own interest﻿—there is another side to this question. Is it fair to Jack to marry him if you do not love him? Is it fair to destroy my happiness as well as your own if you can bring yourself to love me?
Looking at him with a faint impulse of pity.
Mischievously in spite of her pity.
I do. It sounds ridiculous; but it’s no exaggeration. I do; and I always shall.

Always is a long word, Tavy. You see, I shall have to live up always to your idea of my divinity; and I don’t think I could do that if we were married. But if I marry Jack, you’ll never be disillusioned﻿—at least not until I grow too old.
I too shall grow old, Ann. And when I am eighty, one white hair of the woman I love will make me tremble more than the thickest gold tress from the most beautiful young head.
Do you believe that is true?
Tavy, if it is to become true you must lose me as well as love me.
He hastily sits down at the little table and covers his face with his hands.

Oh no you won’t: that wouldn’t be kind. You won’t have a bad time. You will be very nice to women; and you will go a good deal to the opera. A broken heart is a very pleasant complaint for a man in London if he has a comfortable income.
Considerably cooled, but believing that he is only recovering his self-control.
You do not dread disillusionizing Jack.
Her face lighting up with mischievous ecstasy﻿—whispering.
Resuming the calm phase of despair, and beginning to enjoy his broken heart and delicate attitude without knowing it.
Yes: that’s the difficulty, so far.
Well, if it were really agony, would you ask for more of it?
Have I asked for more of it?

You have offered to tell Jack that I love him. That’s self-sacrifice, I suppose; but there must be some satisfaction in it. Perhaps it’s because you’re a poet. You are like the bird that presses its breast against the sharp thorn to make itself sing.
It’s quite simple. I love you; and I want you to be happy. You don’t love me; so I can’t make you happy myself; but I can help another man to do it.

Yes: it seems quite simple. But I doubt if we ever know why we do things. The only really simple thing is to go straight for what you want and grab it. I suppose I don’t love you, Tavy; but sometimes I feel as if I should like to make a man of you somehow. You are very foolish about women.
Then you must keep away from them, and only dream about them. I wouldn’t marry you for worlds, Tavy.
I have no hope, Ann: I accept my ill luck. But I don’t think you quite know how much it hurts.
You are so softhearted! It’s queer that you should be so different from Violet. Violet’s as hard as nails.
Oh no. I am sure Violet is thoroughly womanly at heart.
Something worse﻿—like you! What do you mean, Ann?
Oh well, I don’t mean that, of course. But I have a great respect for Violet. She gets her own way always.
Yes; but somehow she gets it without coaxing﻿—without having to make people sentimental about her.
Oh yes they could, if she made them.
But surely no really nice woman would deliberately practise on men’s instincts in that way.
His passion reviving at the name.
Suppose she were to tell fibs, and lay snares for men?
Hm! Well, at all events, she wouldn’t let you if she were wise. So that’s settled. And now I can’t talk any more. Say you forgive me, and that the subject is closed.
I have nothing to forgive; and the subject is closed. And if the wound is open, at least you shall never see it bleed.
She pats his check; has an impulse to kiss him and then another impulse of distaste which prevents her; finally runs away through the garden and into the villa.
Running to him and lifting his head.
No, no. Who told you about Violet?
Restoring the head to its owner.
But what is it all about? Has Ann been doing anything to you?
It’s not Ann’s fault. And don’t think for a moment that I blame you.
But I haven’t done anything. What’s the matter?
He rises and moves away from her towards the middle of the lawn.
Well, never mind, Tavy. I don’t know which is best for a young man: to know too little, like you, or too much, like Jack.
Well, I’ve disposed of old Malone. I’ve introduced him to Mendoza, Limited; and left the two brigands together to talk it out. Hullo, Tavy! Anything wrong?
He goes his way with sad dignity to the villa.
Yes: life is more complicated than we used to think. But what am I to do for you?
That’s just what I want to tell you. Of course you’ll marry Ann whether I like it myself or not﻿—
No man is a match for a woman, except with a poker and a pair of hobnailed boots. Not always even then. Anyhow, I can’t take the poker to her. I should be a mere slave.
No: she’s afraid of you. At all events, you would tell her the truth about herself. She wouldn’t be able to slip out of it as she does with me.
Everybody would call me a brute if I told Ann the truth about herself in terms of her own moral code. To begin with, Ann says things that are not strictly true.
I’m glad somebody sees she is not an angel.

In short﻿—to put it as a husband would put it when exasperated to the point of speaking out﻿—she is a liar. And since she has plunged Tavy head over ears in love with her without any intention of marrying him, she is a coquette, according to the standard definition of a coquette as a woman who rouses passions she has no intention of gratifying. And as she has now reduced you to the point of being willing to sacrifice me at the altar for the mere satisfaction of getting me to call her a liar to her face, I may conclude that she is a bully as well. She can’t bully men as she bullies women; so she habitually and unscrupulously uses her personal fascination to make men give her whatever she wants. That makes her almost something for which I know no polite name.

I don’t. But what annoys me is that Ann does. I know perfectly well that all this about her being a liar and a bully and a coquette and so forth is a trumped-up moral indictment which might be brought against anybody. We all lie; we all bully as much as we dare; we all bid for admiration without the least intention of earning it; we all get as much rent as we can out of our powers of fascination. If Ann would admit this I shouldn’t quarrel with her. But she won’t. If she has children she’ll take advantage of their telling lies to amuse herself by whacking them. If another woman makes eyes at me, she’ll refuse to know a coquette. She will do just what she likes herself whilst insisting on everybody else doing what the conventional code prescribes. In short, I can stand everything except her confounded hypocrisy. That’s what beats me.
Carried away by the relief of hearing her own opinion so eloquently expressed.
Then why do you want to marry me to her?
Whereas I don’t matter, I suppose.
Oh, you are different, somehow: you are able to take care of yourself. You’d serve her out. And anyhow, she must marry somebody.
Aha! There speaks the life instinct. You detest her; but you feel that you must get her married.
Why, of course I do. What queer things you say, Jack! We can’t help loving our own blood relations.

You shouldn’t say things like that, Jack. I hope you won’t tell Ann that I have been speaking to you. I only wanted to set myself right with you and Tavy. I couldn’t sit mumchance and have everything put on me.
Now don’t be silly and twist what I say into something I don’t mean. I ought to have fair play﻿—
Coming to her mother’s right hand with threatening suavity.
Never fear: Ann is only﻿—well, we were discussing that habit of hers just now. She hasn’t heard a word.
Don’t let him take you to America. Promise me that you won’t.
She chokes, and then breaks out again.
Ann doesn’t care a bit for me.
The sooner you get married too, the better. You will be much less misunderstood.
She takes her towards the villa.
As they go up through the garden.
Violet is quite right. You ought to get married.

Yes, nobody has asked me; but everybody treats the thing as settled. It’s in the air. When we meet, the others go away on absurd pretexts to leave us alone together. Ramsden no longer scowls at me: his eye beams, as if he were already giving you away to me in church. Tavy refers me to your mother and gives me his blessing. Straker openly treats you as his future employer: it was he who first told me of it.
Was that why you ran away?
Yes, only to be stopped by a lovesick brigand and run down like a truant schoolboy.
She turns away from him and sits down, much at her ease.

But why me﻿—me of all men? Marriage is to me apostasy, profanation of the sanctuary of my soul, violation of my manhood, sale of my birthright, shameful surrender, ignominious capitulation, acceptance of defeat. I shall decay like a thing that has served its purpose and is done with; I shall change from a man with a future to a man with a past; I shall see in the greasy eyes of all the other husbands their relief at the arrival of a new prisoner to share their ignominy. The young men will scorn me as one who has sold out: to the young women I, who have always been an enigma and a possibility, shall be merely somebody else’s property﻿—and damaged goods at that: a secondhand man at best.
Well, your wife can put on a cap and make herself ugly to keep you in countenance, like my grandmother.
So that she may make her triumph more insolent by publicly throwing away the bait the moment the trap snaps on the victim!

After all, though, what difference would it make? Beauty is all very well at first sight; but who ever looks at it when it has been in the house three days? I thought our pictures very lovely when papa bought them; but I haven’t looked at them for years. You never bother about my looks: you are too well used to me. I might be the umbrella stand.
You lie, you vampire: you lie.
Flatterer. Why are you trying to fascinate me, Jack, if you don’t want to marry me?
The life force. I am in the grip of the life force.
I don’t understand in the least: it sounds like the Life Guards.
Why don’t you marry Tavy? He is willing. Can you not be satisfied unless your prey struggles?
Turning to him as if to let him into a secret.

What! A man who idolizes women! Who sees nothing in nature but romantic scenery for love duets! Tavy, the chivalrous, the faithful, the tenderhearted and true! Tavy never marry! Why, he was born to be swept up by the first pair of blue eyes he meets in the street.

Yes, I know. All the same, Jack, men like that always live in comfortable bachelor lodgings with broken hearts, and are adored by their landladies, and never get married. Men like you always get married.
Oh, it’s the same with women. The poetic temperament’s a very nice temperament, very amiable, very harmless and poetic, I daresay; but it’s an old maid’s temperament.
Barren. The life force passes it by.
If that’s what you mean by the life force, yes.
And you do care for me?
Rising quietly and shaking her finger at him.
No, a thousand times no: hot water is the revolutionist’s element. You clean men as you clean milk pails, by scalding them.
Cold water has its uses too. It’s healthy.
The will is yours then! The trap was laid from the beginning.
I will not marry you. I will not marry you.
I tell you, no, no, no.
I tell you, yes, yes, yes.
Struck by the echo from the past.
Suddenly losing her courage, with an anguish that she does not conceal.
Well, I made a mistake: you do not love me.
Your happiness will be worth them all.
You would sell freedom and honor and self for happiness?
It will not be all happiness for me. Perhaps death.
Take care, Jack: if anyone comes while we are like this, you will have to marry me.
If we two stood now on the edge of a precipice, I would hold you tight and jump.
Panting, failing more and more under the strain.
Nor I. Let it kill us.
Yes: I don’t care. I am at the end of my forces. I don’t care. I think I am going to faint.
Take care. Something’s the matter with the lady.
He withdraws delicately to the garden steps.
With a sigh of intense relief she relapses.
Yes: I feel strong enough now. But you very nearly killed me, Jack, for all that.
Looking at him with fond pride and caressing his arm.
